title: postgresHasDefault
content: postgresHasDefault Check if default database is available. postgresHasDefault(...) postgresDefault(...) ...Additional arguments passed on to dbConnect() rpsql examples and tests connect to a default database via `dbConnect(`[rpsql::Postgres()]`)`. This function checks if that database is available, and if not, displays an informative message. if (postgresHasDefault()) db <- postgresDefault() print(DBI::dbListTables(db)) DBI::dbDisconnect(db) else message("No database connection.")

title: postgresWaitForNotify
content: postgresWaitForNotify Wait for and return any notifications that return within timeout postgresWaitForNotify(conn, timeout = 1) conna [PqConnection-class] object, produced by [DBI::dbConnect()] timeout How long to wait, in seconds. Default 1 If a notification was available, a list of: channelName of channel pid PID of notifying server process payload Content of notification If no notifications are available, return NULL Once you subscribe to notifications with LISTEN, use this to wait for responses on each channel.

title: postgresIsTransacting
content: postgresIsTransacting Return whether a transaction is ongoing postgresIsTransacting(conn) conna [PqConnection-class] object, produced by [DBI::dbConnect()] A boolean, indicating if a transaction is ongoing. Detect whether the transaction is active for the given connection. A transaction might be started with dbBegin() or wrapped within [DBI::dbWithTransaction()].

title: postgresImportLargeObject
content: postgresImportLargeObject Imports a large object from file postgresImportLargeObject(conn, filepath = NULL, oid = 0) conna [PqConnection-class] object, produced by [DBI::dbConnect()] filepath a path to the large object to import oid the oid to write to. Defaults to 0 which assigns an unused oid the identifier of the large object, an integer Returns an object identifier (Oid) for the imported large object. This function must be called within a transaction. con <- postgresDefault() filepath <- 'your_image.png' dbWithTransaction(con, oid <- postgresImportLargeObject(con, filepath) )

title: postgresExportLargeObject
content: postgresExportLargeObject Exports a large object to file postgresExportLargeObject(conn, oid, filepath) conna [PqConnection-class] object, produced by [DBI::dbConnect()] oid the object identifier (Oid) of the large object to export filepath a path where the large object should be exported invisible NULL on success, or stops with an error Exports a large object from the database to a file on disk. This function uses PostgreSQL's `lo_export()` function which efficiently streams the data directly to disk without loading it into memory, making it suitable for very large objects (GB+) that would cause memory issues with `lo_get()`. This function must be called within a transaction. con <- postgresDefault() filepath <- 'your_image.png' dbWithTransaction(con, oid <- postgresImportLargeObject(con, filepath) ) # Later, export the large object back to a file dbWithTransaction(con, postgresExportLargeObject(con, oid, 'exported_image.png') )

title: Postgres
content: Postgres Connect to a PostgreSQL database 4methoddbConnectPqDriver( drv, dbname = NULL, host = NULL, port = NULL, password = NULL, user = NULL, service = NULL, ..., bigint = c("integer64", "integer", "numeric", "character"), check_interrupts = FALSE, timezone = "UTC", timezone_out = NULL ) 4methoddbDisconnectPqConnection(conn, ...) Postgres() drv[DBI::DBIDriver-class]. Use Postgres() to connect to a PostgreSQL database. Use an existing [DBI::DBIConnection-class] object to clone an existing connection. dbname Database name. If `NULL`, defaults to the user name. Note that this argument can only contain the database name, it will not be parsed as a connection string (internally, `expand_dbname` is set to `false` in the call to [`PQconnectdbParams()`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-connect.html)). user User name and password. If `NULL`, will be retrieved from `PGUSER` and `PGPASSWORD` envvars, or from the appropriate line in `~/.pgpass`. See  for more details. password User name and password. If `NULL`, will be retrieved from `PGUSER` and `PGPASSWORD` envvars, or from the appropriate line in `~/.pgpass`. See  for more details. host Host and port. If `NULL`, will be retrieved from `PGHOST` and `PGPORT` env vars. port Host and port. If `NULL`, will be retrieved from `PGHOST` and `PGPORT` env vars. service Name of service to connect as. If `NULL`, will be ignored. Otherwise, connection parameters will be loaded from the pg_service.conf file and used. See  for details on this file and syntax. ... Other name-value pairs that describe additional connection options as described at  bigint The R type that 64-bit integer types should be mapped to, default is [bit64::integer64], which allows the full range of 64 bit integers. check_interrupts Should user interrupts be checked during the query execution (before first row of data is available)? Setting to `TRUE` allows interruption of queries running too long. timezone Sets the timezone for the connection. The default is `"UTC"`. If `NULL` then no timezone is set, which defaults to the server's time zone. timezone_out The time zone returned to R, defaults to `timezone`. If you want to display datetime values in the local timezone, set to [Sys.timezone()] or `""`. This setting does not change the time values returned, only their display. conn Connection to disconnect. `DBI::dbConnect()` establishes a connection to a database. Set `drv = Postgres()` to connect to a PostgreSQL database Manually disconnecting a connection is not necessary with rpsql, but still recommended; if you delete the object containing the connection, it will be automatically disconnected during the next GC with a warning.

title: A Crash Course on PostgreSQL for R Users
content: Adapted from my blog. Motivation If, like me, you have your workflows that are well organized, even with tidy GitHub repositories and still you create a lot of CSV or RDS files to share periodical data (e.g., weekly or monthly sales), then you can benefit from using PostgreSQL (or any other SQL database engine such as MariaDB). Nycflights13 Let's start with the flights table from the quite popular nycflights13 package: ``r library(nycflights13) flights A tibble: 336,776 × 19 year month day dep_time sched_dep_time dep_delay arr_time sched_arr_time 1 2013 1 1 517 515 2 830 819 2 2013 1 1 533 529 4 850 830 3 2013 1 1 542 540 2 923 850 4 2013 1 1 544 545 -1 1004 1022 5 2013 1 1 554 600 -6 812 837 6 2013 1 1 554 558 -4 740 728 7 2013 1 1 555 600 -5 913 854 8 2013 1 1 557 600 -3 709 723 9 2013 1 1 557 600 -3 838 846 10 2013 1 1 558 600 -2 753 745 ℹ 336,766 more rows ℹ 11 more variables: arr_delay , carrier , flight , tailnum , origin , dest , air_time , distance , hour , minute , time_hour ℹ Use print(n = ...) to see more rows Assume that you work at NYC airport and you are in charge of updating the flights table every day. Instead of creating one CSV file per day with flight records, the process can be better organized by appending new records to an existing SQL table. nycflights13 provides different tables besides flights. You can explore the details in R4DS. Because R4DS, a great book, uses the Tidyverse, here I will use data.table to show something similar in a different way. The relation between the nycflights13 tables is summarised in the following diagram: SQL indexes Skipping a lot of details, SQL creates copies of the tables that contain just a few columns which help to identify observations in order to be able to filter those observations in a faster way that without an index. For example, in the month table, the year column is really useful to create an index that boosts the speed of SQL operations similar to this dplyr statement: `r library(data.table) flights <- as.data.table(flights) flights[month == 3] year month day dep_time sched_dep_time dep_delay arr_time 1: 2013 3 1 4 2159 125 318 2: 2013 3 1 50 2358 52 526 3: 2013 3 1 117 2245 152 223 4: 2013 3 1 454 500 -6 633 5: 2013 3 1 505 515 -10 746 --- 28830: 2013 3 31 2349 2355 -6 333 28831: 2013 3 31 2358 2359 -1 332 28832: 2013 3 31 NA 1627 NA NA 28833: 2013 3 31 NA 600 NA NA 28834: 2013 3 31 NA 929 NA NA sched_arr_time arr_delay carrier flight tailnum origin dest air_time 1: 56 142 B6 11 N706JB JFK FLL 166 2: 438 48 B6 707 N794JB JFK SJU 198 3: 2354 149 B6 608 N328JB JFK PWM 48 4: 648 -15 US 1117 N177US EWR CLT 79 5: 810 -24 UA 475 N527UA EWR IAH 199 --- 28830: 338 -5 B6 707 N657JB JFK SJU 202 28831: 339 -7 B6 727 N608JB JFK BQN 195 28832: 1734 NA EV 4299 N17560 EWR DCA NA 28833: 725 NA EV 5689 N829AS LGA IAD NA 28834: 1220 NA UA 1597 EWR EGE NA distance hour minute time_hour 1: 1069 21 59 2013-03-01 21:00:00 2: 1598 23 58 2013-03-01 23:00:00 3: 273 22 45 2013-03-01 22:00:00 4: 529 5 0 2013-03-01 05:00:00 5: 1400 5 15 2013-03-01 05:00:00 --- 28830: 1598 23 55 2013-03-31 23:00:00 28831: 1576 23 59 2013-03-31 23:00:00 28832: 199 16 27 2013-03-31 16:00:00 28833: 229 6 0 2013-03-31 06:00:00 28834: 1725 9 29 2013-03-31 09:00:00 To create indexes, let's start differentiating between unique and non-unique indexes: `r unique_index <- list( airlines = list("carrier"), planes = list("tailnum") ) index <- list( airports = list("faa"), flights = list(c("year", "month", "day"), "carrier", "tailnum", "origin", "dest"), weather = list(c("year", "month", "day"), "origin") ) SQL conections Assume the following: The NYC airport gave you access to a PostgreSQL database named rpsql_test. You have VPN access to it from 127.0.0.1 (or localhost) on port 5432. The user is and the password is S4cr3tP4ssw0rd007. Important: Database credentials (e.g., user and password) should be stored in your ~/.Rprofile and never in your scripts! You can use nano, vim or just usethis::edit_r_environ() to edit your R profile to add the credentials and then restart your R session to apply the changes. The file should be of the form: `bash PGDATABASE="rpsql_test" PGPORT=5432 PGUSER="postgres" PGPASSWORD="S4cr3tP4ssw0rd007" To access and start creating tables to better organize your data, you need to open and close conections, and the rpsql package is really useful to do that and more: `r library(DBI) library(rpsql) fun_connect <- function() { dbconect( Postgres(), dbname = Sys.getenv("PGDATABASE"), user = Sys.getenv("PGUSER"), password = Sys.getenv("PGPASSWORD"), host = "localhost" ) } By default, PostgreSQL uses the public schema in a databases, which you'll write to. You can explore the existing tables in the public schema of postgres database by running: `r schema <- "public" con <- fun_connect() remote_tables <- dbGetQuery( con, sprintf("SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='%s'", schema) ) dbDisconnect(con) remote_tables <- as.character(remote_tables$table_name) remote_tables character(0) Because this is an example with a freshly created server just for the tutorial, the result is no existing tables in the database. Creating tables Now you should be ready to start writing the tables from nycflights13 to the database: `r local_tables <- utils::data(package = "nycflights13")$results[, "Item"] tables <- setdiff(local_tables, remote_tables) for (table in tables) { df <- getExportedValue("nycflights13", table) message("Creating table: ", table) table_name <- table con <- fun_connect() dbWriteTable(con, table_name, df) dbDisconnect(con) } Creating table: airlines Creating table: airports Creating table: flights Creating table: planes Creating table: weather This approach prevents overwriting in case that a table already exists, you can pass overwrite = TRUE to dbWriteTable(), but instead this appends new observations. For the indexes previously defined as lists, one possibility is: `r con <- fun_connect() for (table in names(unique_index)) { for (columns in unique_index[[table]]) { col_str <- paste(columns, collapse = ", ") idx_name <- sprintf("unique_%s_%s", table, paste(columns, collapse = "_")) sql <- sprintf("CREATE UNIQUE INDEX %s ON %s (%s)", idx_name, table, col_str) dbExecute(con, sql) } } for (table in names(index)) { for (columns in index[[table]]) { col_str <- paste(columns, collapse = ", ") idx_name <- sprintf("idx_%s_%s", table, paste(columns, collapse = "_")) sql <- sprintf("CREATE INDEX %s ON %s (%s)", idx_name, table, col_str) dbExecute(con, sql) } } dbDisconnect(con) Accessing tables Let's say you need to count the observations per month and save the result locally: `r con <- fun_connect() obs_per_month <- dbGetQuery(con, "select year, month, count() as n from flights group by year, month") dbDisconnect(con) obs_per_month year month n 1 2013 1 27004 2 2013 2 24951 3 2013 3 28834 4 2013 4 28330 5 2013 5 28796 6 2013 6 28243 7 2013 7 29425 8 2013 8 29327 9 2013 9 27574 10 2013 10 28889 11 2013 11 27268 12 2013 12 28135 The result of the query is a data.frame, which can be saved as CSV file with, among other possibilities as any other local dataset. Appending new records Let's say you have a table flights14 with records for the year 2014. To append those records to the existing flights table in the database, you need to run: `r con <- fun_connect() dbWriteTable(con, "flights", flights14, append = TRUE, overwrite = FALSE, row.names = FALSE) dbDisconnect(con) Appending large tables Let's say your flights14 contains 12,345,678 rows. A better approach than writing the full table at once is to divide it in parts of 2,500,000 rows (or another smaller number). Using base R ``r N <- 2500000 starts <- seq(1L, nrow(flights14), by = N) con <- fun_connect() for (j in seq_along(starts)) { message(sprintf("Writing fragment %s of %s", j, length(starts))) end <- min(starts[j] + N - 1L, nrow(flights14)) dbWriteTable(con, "flights", flights14[starts[j]:end], append = TRUE, overwrite = FALSE, row.names = FALSE) } dbDisconnect(con)
